cap.n0: The paper that started it all was about translation.|Today's big chatbots threw away half of its design.
cap.n1: From Lecture 2 of Professor Yufei|Ding's CSE 291P at UC San Diego.
cap.n2: The paper: Attention Is All You Need, 2017.|Its model, the Transformer, was built to translate:|a sentence in, its translation out.
cap.n3: The encoder reads the sentence;|the decoder writes the translation.
cap.n4: Picture a team at one desk: a reader and a writer.
cap.n5: He reads a sentence in a made-up language.|She writes the translation: I am a student.
cap.n6: Before 2017,|the best translators were mostly recurrent networks.
cap.n7: A recurrent network reads one word after another,|like a whisper passed down a line: one step per word.
cap.n8: The 2017 paper dropped recurrence and kept only attention.|Hence the title.
cap.n9: Attention is a round table.|Each word asks: which of the others are like me?|It gathers from them, weighted by that, and updates itself.
cap.n10: Unlike the whisper line,|all the words do this in the same step,|so a GPU can work on them at the same time.
cap.n11: The reader uses attention:|every word can look at every other word,|before and after it.
cap.n12: Models read text in tokens: words or pieces of words.|Professor Ding:
cap.c2: So even the first token can look at the third token.|And the second token can also look at the third token.|So it's bidirectional for the encoding part.
cap.n13: Writing, though, is still one word at a time,|and each new word joins the input for the next.
cap.n14: Before each word, she reads his notes on the whole input.|That is cross-attention.
cap.n15: That's the 2017 team.|Professor Ding's advice for reading an older paper:
cap.c1: you can always ask yourself,|can you predict what is the trend afterwards?|And can you improve that paper?
cap.n16b: Most of today's large chat models that|publish their design keep only the decoder.|They fired the reader.
cap.n17: Slide 11 of the lecture shades the cut in red.|Delete the encoder.|The cross-attention has nothing left to look at,|so it goes too.
cap.n18: What stays: the decoder alone.|It's called decoder-only.
cap.n19: Alone, the writer keeps the rule she always had:|a card hides the rest of her strip.
cap.n20: Each word may look at itself and the words before it,|never ahead. That's called masked, or causal, attention.
cap.n21: So how does she translate now?|Write the request at the start of her page.|It came first, so the card never hides it,|and she simply continues the text.
cap.n22: What does she lose? Try this: The bank was full of fish.
cap.n23: When she reaches “bank”, the card hides the fish.|Money, or river? The reader saw the whole sentence at once.
cap.n24: Why read both ways at all? Professor Ding:
cap.c3: Because if you look at the translation example,|at least we believe for the translation,|we should look at the whole sentence.
cap.n25: Looking only backward can hurt on some understanding tasks.
cap.n26: So why accept a less exact model?|Professor Ding's slide 12 keeps the books.
cap.c4: So we are losing something.|But we are gaining something.
cap.n27: First gain: one stack instead of two.
cap.n28: The numbers a model learns are called parameters,|or weights.|Each half is a stack of layers; two stacks carry more:|about 1.5 to 2 times, the slide estimates.
cap.n29: By our count, that cut takes the 2017 base model from about|63 million parameters to about 38 million: about 40% fewer.
cap.n31: To learn translation directly you need pairs:|a sentence and its translation.|That's paired data. The 2017 model learned from about|4.5 million sentence pairs.
cap.n32: A next-word model, like our writer, can learn from any text:|hide the next word, guess it, check.
cap.n33: GPT-3 read about 300 billion tokens;|Llama 3, about 15 trillion.
cap.n34: One honest limit. A 2022 study found next-word models best|right after training on plain text,|but two-stack models ahead after|extra training on many tasks.
cap.n35: And two-stack models still show up in translation.
cap.n36: So which is better?|Professor Ding asks the question students ask:
cap.c5: when you should do accurate modeling|and when you should do simple modeling?
cap.n37: Accurate: the team, reading both ways.|Simple: the lone writer, any text.
cap.n38: Remember episode one: scale changes what models can do.|The simple design that scales won, for now.|Nobody has proven it is the best design.
cap.c6: Because it's always alternating between each other.|No clean winner.
cap.n40: Most of today's big chat models kept only the writer:|she never peeks ahead, but any text is practice.
cap.n41: Next time you read an older paper,|try Professor Ding's test: guess what comes after it.
